utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to our sound engineers, the interpreters; I hope you hear me. Good morning to counsel for the Prosecution and for the Defence, to General Krstic. We are here for the hearing in the case of General Krstic. I believe there were two points which the Defence wished to raise last week. Are you ready now, Mr. Visnjic, to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I think we have a problem here. I am not getting the French interpretation. Yes, I seem to be on the right channel. Now it's all right. Now it is all right. Very well. We always have problems of communication, don't we? Mr. Visnjic, I believe we have established contact now. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. I should also like to say good morning to our learned friends from the Prosecution, to the registry, to our interpreters and sound engineers. Mr. President, the two issues I wish to raise arose during a closed session of the hearing. I do not know if this is a public session. If it is, perhaps it would be advisable to go into a closed session briefly because of the two questions I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are now in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are in a public session, but we shall now move to a closed session so that Mr. Visnjic could raise these issues. Would there be any interest in addressing these questions in a public session, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. These are technical issues, more or less, but in view of the nature of the problem, I believe it will be more advisable if we closed it to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If there are reasons to go into a closed session, then we shall do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to have face distortion, as requested by the witness, we are going to keep the public character of the hearing only through the audio transmission, and it is possible to follow the proceedings only in the room which is situated next to the press office. This is a public hearing; however, there will be nobody -- there will be no public in the small room here on my right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Dubuisson. We are ready. The witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness D. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that you've had a nice weekend here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was not exactly nice, but it was okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well, then. In any case, we are going to do our best to have you feel comfortable here. Let me just remind you that you are still under oath. You have requested certain protective measures, and they will be applied. There will be nobody in the public gallery in this courtroom, and the public will be able to follow the proceedings in one other room here at the Tribunal. Witness D, you will now continue with giving answers to the counsel for the Defence, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness D, I should like to go back to the month of July 1995. Could you please tell the Chamber what your occupation was at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, because I had been wounded, I didn't have any particular occupation. I was at home, and I was receiving treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At that time, Witness D, were you a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the 11th of July, 1995. You testified that on that day, you had left Srebrenica for Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe your departure from Srebrenica to Potocari to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left on foot. My house was not very far from Potocari, and I left on foot together with my wife and my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were there many people on the road on that day, going from Srebrenica to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the road was crowded with people, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us whether this column of people going towards Potocari was exposed to any shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, there was some shelling; however, I cannot be sure whether the column itself was targeted. There were lots of shells falling in the vicinity of the road which was taken by those people, and as far as I heard from other people, there was some shelling but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You testified during your direct examination that on the 12th of July, in the factory where you had found accommodation, some Serb soldiers appeared; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You told us that they were dressed in a different fashion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you also said that they spoke with a different accent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that I observed personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that they sounded as if they were from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with the various accents from the former Yugoslavia because I used to travel a lot. I knew accents from Macedonia, Montenegro, and so on, and I had many friends all around the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was the dialect in question the Ijekavica dialect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm sure you're familiar with this special accent that is used in Montenegro. There is something very particular about it, and people from that area can understand each other perfectly, and it is an easily recognisable accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you distinguish between the two variants of the language, between Ijekavica and Ekavica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I should perhaps emphasise that they spoke with the so-called Ekavica. But in addition to that, there were some -- there was something particular which indicated to me that those people were from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you one more question. Before you testified here, before this Chamber, you gave a number of statements, including the statement that you gave to the police, or rather to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement before this Chamber, the one that you gave on Friday, you mentioned a person by the name of Garic, and some sabotage activity he had been involved with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I have noticed that you did not mention this particular event in your previous statements. Could you please tell me why are you mentioning it only now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question? I don't think I mentioned Garic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the incident in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is normal for the statement to contain a number of details, and the reason why I didn't mention it before -- well, there's nothing special. I did have a conversation with a man by the name of Spomenko, and he wanted to tell me about this particular action. He wanted, actually, me to confirm what he was saying, and his name was not Spomenko, but Stanimir. He wanted me to tell him about that particular action, he insisted on it, so I told him about it. And, indeed, this action had taken place. Everybody knew about it. You can ask anyone in Srebrenica, and they will all confirm you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just one

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness D.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would just like to understand more clearly how you detected these people, the soldiers which you mentioned spoke the Ekavica dialect, and you were able to conclude that they came from Montenegro. Now, in Bosnia, don't you speak different dialects, or is it usually that nobody speaks another dialect from other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain this to you, Your Honour, and I will try to be brief. As I have just told you, I used to travel a lot throughout the former Yugoslavia, and I had a number of friends everywhere. I had an encounter with those soldiers; they wanted to see my ID; they wanted to know where I had been wounded, and I told them that I had been wounded before. So that conversation lasted for a while, several minutes probably, and I could tell that they were speaking the Ekavica dialect. This dialect can be spoken by people in Bosnia and in Serbia, of course; however, there is something particular about that kind of accent when it's coming from a Montenegro, and that's how I managed to detect that. My conclusion was that the soldiers were from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, if I remember rightly, your testimony before the weekend, you did not only mention that they had different dialect, you mentioned that they looked different, they were dressed differently than those from around Srebrenica. Am I remembering rightly, or was it just the dialect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you are right, Your Honour. They had camouflage uniforms, that is, multi-coloured uniforms, but they were somehow better quality. You can distinguish between uniforms in terms of quality. Serbian soldiers whom we could see in the area, that is, in the vicinity of the lines around Srebrenica, had uniforms of somewhat worse quality, and these other soldiers had better uniforms, they looked better. Let me try to explain. You have various types of camouflage uniforms, depending on the army, that is, the country the soldiers in question are coming from, and people tend to compare uniforms. And I thought that their uniforms were of a somewhat better quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Only the quality, or was it the badge too or any sign that showed that they belonged to the army of Serbia, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice the insignia. Probably because of my fear, I didn't observe carefully. It was just a general impression. I did not pay particular attention to their insignia, and I cannot say that I observed the insignia. It was only the quality and type of uniform that I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And their accent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the accent as well, this specific kind of speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Also in your testimony last Friday, I think, you spoke of this young, beautiful girl who -- there was a whole thing, but at the end, she was taken away, and you heard screams. Did you know after that what happened to this girl? Did she come back? Did she relate anything? Was she -- did she survive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't learn anything on that day, neither could I do so on the following days, but when I reached the free territory in Kladanj, the BH army wanted to take my statement, they wanted to know what I had been through. So after I had given my statement and after I had mentioned the young woman in my statement, they told me that they knew about the girl and that she was alive, and they told me that she had been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did she confess -- did she say anything about what happened to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything else. I don't know her name. Maybe the whole thing remained her secret. I didn't inquire about the girl further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a last question. I understood, perhaps rightly, that you were wounded, and for this purpose, perhaps you did not continue the war; is that right? When were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded at the very beginning of the war. I had sustained serious injuries, and the treatment was quite difficult. You probably know that there were no medicines in Srebrenica at the time. The wound would often get infected, and I had a lot of problems with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then you completely left any military activity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely. There were a number of soldiers who were healthy, but they left the army as well because of the demilitarisation. There was no need for them. And I was not capable to join anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness D.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness D, I have three questions. Number 1, when you were taken off the bus in Luka, did anybody ask you about whether you were wounded or whether you were disabled in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked me that question. I was simply pulled back by the shoulder and ordered to give my child to my wife. I was carrying my daughter, but I had to follow the soldier who had ordered me to give her to my wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My second question is you describe the different dialect and uniforms of the soldiers who were around the factory in Potocari. Was that true of all the soldiers, or were there some local soldiers? Were all the soldiers that you were able to come into contact with around Potocari of this different variety of uniform and dialect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that that was the only group of Serbian soldiers with whom I had any contact. I could only observe others, and I didn't have any contact with other soldiers. So I cannot say anything as to their belonging to any particular group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to make sure I understand. You may have seen other soldiers, but you weren't close enough to them to know what they were, or you didn't see any soldiers at all that were not of the Montenegrin variety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a couple of those soldiers, those who had this other type of uniform which I mentioned, and I also saw a number of soldiers who were wearing this uniform that was -- the one that I described as of somewhat worse quality. I did see a number of other soldiers, but that was the only group that I had actually talked to, and I had to talk to them because they wanted to see my ID. And I should say that they behaved decently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is, when you were taken off the bus in Luka and taken to the school with 22 other men, and later taken to the field for execution, did you have an opportunity to find out where those other men had come from? In other words, had they been taken off buses, or had they been captured or surrendered from the column that was marching toward Tuzla? The other men that were with you in the field and in the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question, Your Honour. I was able to find out, yes. Serb soldiers talked to a number of people. Fuad and Alija, whose names I mentioned, for example, had set out in the direction of the wood, so they were captured on the way through the woods, whereas other people, they were all from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So they came from both people who had stayed in Potocari and people who had gone off with the column that marched towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness D, you have heard a number of questions from everybody here, from the Prosecution, from the Defence, from the Judges. Is there anything else you wish to say to the Chamber, something you haven't yet said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have so many things to say, to talk about, but I don't know, I don't think there is anything in particular that I should like to add to my statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness D, let me thank you on behalf of the Chamber for coming here to testify, to testify about the suffering and the ordeal you have been through. I do hope that you will be able to have a number of nice weekends once you come back to your country. Thank you once again for coming here to testify, and the usher will now help you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I was really delighted to testify here, and I was impressed by the attitude of all of the participants here in the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, the next witness, is he a protected witness? No. But perhaps this would be a convenient time to make the break. So do not call him in yet. I'm just wondering if --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed by Mr. McCloskey, who will lead the next witness, that he is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What kind of protection does he seek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Face distortion and no name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why is he seeking protection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He told me that his -- he's got a large family that would like to move back to the area some day and that he's concerned about his family and the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Does the Defence agree with the protective measures for the witness? Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, we do agree in the case of protective measures, but we do agree, we have no objection against protective measures here, except that now it occurs to me perhaps it might be good to contact, to communicate, before the witness comes in, but that, again, is a matter between the Prosecution and the Defence. So before a witness comes in perhaps -- before whatever witness comes in, we should like to have contact with the Prosecution and discuss it. But in this case, yes, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Will, then, the counsel for the Prosecution, bear this in mind, and keep in contact with the Defence. We shall now make a 20-minute break, and in order to expedite matters, I should like to ask Mr. Dubuisson to bring in the witness before the Judges have entered the courtroom. A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Witness E, we shall now go into closed session so that we can regulate the question of identity of the witness. Are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. Witness E, thank you for coming here. As you know, we have taken all the measures to protect you. We shall not be pronouncing your name and we shall call you Witness E. Please make yourself comfortable. Now, Witness E, you will answer questions which the Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, will put to you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness E, how are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Fine. Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you a little bit nervous?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't but be nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll be asking you some questions, and so will the Defence and so will the Court, and we shouldn't be here too long.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In Subin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when were you born? What's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Subin in the Srebrenica opstina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you grow up around there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you do woodcutting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you live on July 11th, the day that Srebrenica fell to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who you did you live with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: With my family; (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When the Serb troops attacked, we left and went to UNPROFOR, near the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: And from there, we headed for Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that with your group, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what about your son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He stayed behind in Srebrenica, and I don't know where he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were the ages of your daughters? Just roughly what was the age range of your daughters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about your grandchildren? About how old were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The eldest one was three years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you got to Potocari, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We went to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one of the hangars did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The one that belonged to Transport, for car/truck washing, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the bus company Transport or the Express Bus Compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We did, on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the 12th, what did you do, the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: On the 12th, I went down from the place where they cleaned and washed buses and cars. There were about 500 of us in that hangar, and until sometime, 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see Serb soldiers at any time while you were in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. What's his name? Milisav Gavric entered from the opposite side into the hangar. And Ibran Mustafic and Hamid, he went to them and tapped them on their shoulder, and they talked. I don't know what they talked about really. And then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, how did you know Milisav Gavric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Milisav Gavric was with the police, and he came for some training with the forestry company before he changed his mind and went to work for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he worked for the police before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That day that you saw him in the hangar, can you describe what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He had something like blue, like SMB, I cannot tell you exactly what, but I think he had that kind of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any other Bosnian Serbs come into the hangar besides Milisav Gavric that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I did not see anyone come in or leave the hangar. When Milisav left, when he was gone, then after some time ten minutes, he came back, Milisav Gavric and Mladic came, and they took Ibran and Hamid and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I went to the door straight away. People in the hangar were puzzled. And we came out, and when I came to the stairs, then I saw some Serb troops, some seven or eight soldiers. And we crossed the bridge and boarded old buses or trucks -- I mean trailers, and that is where I spent the night with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you take your family to these old trailers or buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, just in case, you know, all sorts of things happen. If it rained, that was one thing. Secondly, to shelter my family if anything happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you want them out of that hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, because we were afraid. We didn't know what might come to pass that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were these old buses that you're talking about, were they running, or were they just derelict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. No, they were broken buses, derelict, discarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have the whole family, all your daughters and your grandchildren and your wife, with you in one of those structures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, all of us, all of us in that ancient truck trailer. Everybody was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where was this truck trailer in relation to the bus hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, right as you come out from the hangar and cross the bridge, closer to the asphalt, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it was between the asphalt road and the bus hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that night like? Can you describe that night in that structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Oh, yes, how we spent the night, I can tell you. It was so horrible that you couldn't -- you couldn't really go down on the ground because of the screams, because of the noise, because of the havoc. You couldn't really have a moment's peace from fear and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do when morning came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When the day broke, I got up to go down to the stream, to relieve myself, and when I crossed that road, which was behind the trailer, down to the stream, I looked and saw 11 dead, and I started back, but then I stopped again because I was so frightened, and I thought, "Well, let's see who that is." And when I looked, I saw (redacted) dead, six women and five men. Then I went back up to the hangar and went to the trailer, and I immediately took my children and my wife and said, "Let's get ready and go. I'm not spending another night here."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about how far away this little creek was from where you were in the -- where you'd spent the night in this structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: About ten metres, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you came back and found your family, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The children and the wife, that is, the family of mine, I told them to get ready and go to the asphalt and then to go on to the roadblock, to the ramp, and see how far we can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I did that. We started at 6.00 and we came out onto the asphalt, and until 9.15, we could not reach the ramp. At quarter past nine, we arrived at the ramp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the ramp that you described near where people were getting on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, it was right up there, and to the right where buses and trucks to transport people, such as population and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened when you got your family to that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When I arrived at the ramp, there were two Serb soldiers and to answer, next to the APCs where the rope was tied. And they opened it. I passed, we passed, and my neighbour (redacted) followed but he was stopped right there, he was separated, and I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who separated him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: A Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was your brother anywhere near the vicinity at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Right exactly behind (redacted) is where he was, and he was also separated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you seen your neighbour (redacted) or your brother since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: And from there I started towards the buses. First there were trucks, then there were buses parked, and I reached the third truck and a Serb soldier waved a hand at me and said, "The first bus." And I went on, down the asphalt road, and then some time later, I looked to my left and on the left side I saw Sreten and his uncle, and that one from the Izvoriste, what's his name, Maksimovic, there, and with him was Mikinovac from Polomovci. And they were talking next to the asphalt, on the left-hand side, and I passed by them and got to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you know Sreten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Oh, well, I knew Sreten (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how old was Sreten at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: About 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was Sreten's father's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was Ilija known to be from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not see Ilija there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But can you just tell me, if you know, where Ilija was from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: From Spat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there anything unique about Ilija's appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, he had a long moustache hanging down. He was paying to have a moustache -- to wear a moustache like this. So one could always recognise him. Whoever knew him could recognise him anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know Sreten's last name now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't remember. I've forgotten that. I knew that but I've forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was Sreten wearing at the time you saw him by the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you tell what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was just standing and talking to his -- to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These other people you described, were they in uniform also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In uniforms also, and they were talking. For instance, I passed by as they were talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do as you passed by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I got to the bus, I went onto the bus, and I sat there. When a young man appeared and he wanted to board the bus, and the driver wouldn't open the door to him, indicating with his hand to go to the left, to where the driver's window is. And this man went to the driver's window and they talked about something, but I couldn't hear what they were talking about. And then he passed by the bus and I recognised him as Sreten's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was Sreten's son wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: A uniform also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: And then we waited for the buses. The buses switched on but we did not start, but after about half an hour, we started to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any other men on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, there were seven others. I was the eighth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know about how old the other seven were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, they were all my senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did the bus go when it finally left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It started towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did it go after Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: And then on to Kravica, Glogova, Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see anything along the way in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, nothing until we reached Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what did you see at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When we arrived in Kravica, to my left, I saw our men dead, and then some ten metres further on, we saw our men in front of the bus with their hands like this [indicates], behind their neck, and that they were moving towards buses. Then we moved on another 50 metres, and a small flag was put up and the bus stopped. The driver wouldn't stop, and he raised this little flag three times, and then he opened just one part of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If I can interrupt you for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, the witness said that he saw "our men with their hands behind their neck," and he put his hands behind his neck briefly, as we can all imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, are you Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you refer to "our men," you're referring to Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how many Muslim men did you see with their hands behind their necks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There must have been about 100, if not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know what they were doing. They had been captured and brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they walking or were they sitting, or how did you actually see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were walking towards the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Then we passed by those men, they stayed behind, and then some ten metres on, to the right, there were about 20 or 30 men standing and some three or four Serb soldiers standing by them. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So those 20 or 30 men you saw standing, were those Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then what else did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: And I only saw the armament, I saw a tank and three armoured vehicles, which were covered there. I couldn't really see which ones were they. And on our way between Kravica and Konjevic Polje, I saw yet another man of ours dead, next to the asphalt on the left-hand side, and then I saw nothing else until we reached Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you reached the intersection near Konjevic Polje, which way did the bus turn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Towards -- what villages are in that direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Towards Nova Kasaba, that's where we went. And when I looked to my left, above Taran's cafe, in his meadow, there were 200 or 300 of our men lying down, and there were about 10, or maybe 20 Serb soldiers walking around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how long in distance after you turned left towards Nova Kasaba did you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. These men lying down. He means dead or lying down? What is the meaning of "lying down"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you clarify your answer for the Judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Alive. Alive. They waved at us. They were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about how far after you turned left at the intersection did you see these men in this meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, about ten metres from Taran's cafe, they were right there, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Then we headed for Nova Kasaba and Milici and Vlasenica, and we arrived in Tisca and got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then did you and your family walk to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Seven kilometres from Tisca to Kladanj on foot, I and my whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Witness E, you are now going to be asked questions that will be put to you by the Defence. I think that it is going to be Mr. Visnjic who will cross-examine you. Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness E.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you had arrived in Srebrenica on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I left Srebrenica for Potocari on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise and tell us what exactly was happening on that first night in Potocari, between the 11th and the 12th? Were there any specific events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, there were no special events, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 11th of July, your son did not go with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know. He simply stayed behind, and I don't know what happened with him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, you described an event involving Gavric and Mladic. They came to the hangar, and they were looking for Ibrahim Mustafic. Who is Ibrahim Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He is a man from Potocari. He's a local person, and I didn't know anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were Gavric and Mladic alone, or was there anyone else with them when they came to get Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were two soldiers standing on the stairs at the moment they came in, and later on those two soldiers went with them. But I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How far was that stairway from the spot where Ibran was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, the stairs were at the entrance of the hangar. There was a corridor without any opening, but I couldn't tell you exactly how far it was from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: More than 20 metres perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, yes, around 20 metres. Between 20 and 25 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "Mladic," you refer to General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did Mladic say anything when they came to get Ibrahim Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. Whether he told him something or not, I couldn't -- I couldn't exactly tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that something had happened on the night between the 12th and the 13th of July, and I should like to ask you a question about that. You said you had seen 11 bodies in the water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I'm not saying anything I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific as to the time when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It was about 5.30 a.m. when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I could only recognise my neighbour, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you conclude anything about the cause of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I didn't see who had killed them, so I couldn't tell you anything about the cause of their death.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, you gave statements to the Tribunal and to the Commission for Gathering Facts on War Crimes in the Territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina on a previous occasion. Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could please show the statement to the witness, the statement he gave on a previous occasion. This is the statement given by the witness to the State Commission for Gathering Facts on War Crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. This witness will not be able to read, so it may be best if you read particular portions to him. He apparently left his glasses back at home.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understood, Mr. McCloskey, the witness cannot read. So what is actually the case? Is it because he cannot read at the moment, or is it because he doesn't read at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know he cannot read because he cannot see very well. He has told me he can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Let us bear this fact in mind, Mr. Visnjic. I think you had better read the statement to the witness, and then the witness will give you his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement is a handwritten document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, but let me please draw your attention to the confidential character of the document, which contains the name of the witness as well. So we should avoid reading any identifying elements of this witness, or perhaps we could go into a private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Dubuisson. In this statement, Mr. Visnjic, are you going to mention the name of the witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the name is mentioned in this statement, but it's not mentioned in the paragraph I'm about to read. His name is not contained in this particular paragraph. However, the fact that the statement was given by him is stated in this statement. His name is on the statement but not in the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm right, this means that even if the statement contains the witness's name, it will have to be tendered under seal. Am I right, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Your Honour. I suppose that Mr. Visnjic will ask for this document to be filed as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. You may continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in page 4 of the Serbo-Croatian version of the statement, that is, the last portion of the paragraph, last portion of the text, on page 3 in the English version. The text is as follows: Once again, I will be reading from the fourth line of page 4 of the Serbo-Croatian text. "Sreten is about 30 years old. His cousin is a little younger. He slit the throats of 13 people in Tengara and threw them in the Drina River. I saw them slaughter 11 people with my own eyes, and I saw Sreten. They were slaughtering people who were standing up. They just passed by and slit their throats with a knife. There were three more individuals besides Sreten. Of the victims, I know

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: (redacted). Of the victims, there were five men and six women. There were no children. They used black army knives for the killing."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a statement which this witness gave on the 19th -- that is, on the 17th of August, 1995, immediately after the relevant events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, could you please tell me whether the text that I have just read to you is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, sir. I never gave such a statement. I know what I said, and I'm giving the same testimony here today. I cannot confirm that statement as my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, from what the Prosecutor has told us, I can conclude that you have some trouble with your sight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can't see very well. I have had this problem for two or three years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when the situation in respect of your sight worsened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Two or three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So at the time you gave this statement, in 1995, you could see very well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are in a situation here. I cannot show him his signature, the one that is on this particular statement, and I cannot ask him questions about it. I cannot find out whether this, indeed, is his signature because he doesn't have glasses. However, I should perhaps ask Witness E whether he remembers giving this statement to the said State Commission.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't remember ever giving such a statement. As so what is contained in there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, do you remember how many statements you have given so far?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I remember giving a statement on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you gave the first one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who you gave this statement to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, at the end of this particular statement, one can see the following words: "Statement given by," then we can see your name, and then just below your name, we can read "The witness cannot see."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This statement was given on 17th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In 1995, sir, I could see. My sight got worse within the past two or three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, you told us you had worked as a woodcutter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you spent a great deal of time in nature, in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Woodcutters usually work during summertime.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When is the busiest period of the year for you as a woodcutter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, we cut wood both in winter time and summer time. The season was always good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me about the time of the day when it dawns in your country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I forgot about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, do you remember giving a statement to the investigator of the Tribunal in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember. I don't remember about giving statements to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me introduce this. This is a statement given by the witness to the investigators of the Tribunal in October 1998. This is the English version. I apologise to the B/C/S booth, I don't have that one, but I shall try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is marked as D4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same event; that is, the one you described to this Chamber when you saw 11 bodies in the water, six women and five men, because we're in the same situation as with the previous statement. I shall read the relevant portion to you. "Early in the morning, around 3.00 in the morning, I went over to the creek to urinate and I counted 11 bodies, six women and five men, lying in the creek. I recognised (redacted) among them. All of them had been stabbed at the side of their throat. Their throats were not cut. I have never told (redacted) family that I saw him there." Witness E, is this correct, what I have just read out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I cannot confirm anything as to the issue with the families. It's a very sad thing, and you cannot speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you went to the creek to urinate around 3.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I told you when I went to urinate. I don't know about this statement. I don't know who wrote this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, did you sign this statement that was taken on the 10th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness E, could you be more specific about your problems with your sight? Is it that you cannot see very well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I cannot see very well, that is the case. It is all foggy in front of my eyes. It's very difficult for me to make out a silhouette in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness E.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you see me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I can hardly see you. I mean, it's very difficult for me to see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When did you start having these problems of not seeing? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, during the past two years, I started having this problem. There are always tears in my eyes, and I have problems with my sight. I can't see very well now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it the result of any accident or disease? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, it's not a disease. I connect this problem with all the psychological problems that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you also have memory problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. I often have headaches and I have memory problems. It's very difficult for me to remember things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you remember the certain things which you told us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, these are the things that I remember very well, but if you ask me about things happening now, sometimes I tend to forget them within two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, you forgot that you signed the statement which you gave -- which apparently you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal. You forgot that completely.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you forgot what was in it too, because usually you meet the investigators. Did you also forget meeting them? I beg your pardon? You forgot meeting the investigators and telling them anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: You mean here, after I've arrived here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No. On 10 October 1998, in 1998, two years ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember. I don't remember being with an investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Anyhow, in the statement which you don't remember, you said partly the same thing you said today, that you saw down the stream 11 dead persons, but in the statement, you were more explicit, you said there were six women and five men, stabbed at the side of the throat. So you had more details. But the fact remains that you mentioned the same number, which is 11 dead persons. Do you remember that clearly, that there were 11 dead persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I remember 11. There were 11 of them, six women and five men. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, then, the statement was not wrong, because you are repeating it today. And were they also stabbed in the side of the neck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, they were. In the neck, that's where they were stabbed. I know about that, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You do remember that. And what kind of women were they? Were they dressed in uniform, in military uniform, or were they just housewives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Housewives. Housewives. Not a single one of them wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned also that you saw 100 persons or more with their hands tied behind their neck, walking to the bus. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember seeing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And did you know anybody among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I couldn't recognise anyone because, you know, the bus was moving and I had no time to recognise anyone. I was on the bus and I just couldn't recognise people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just something in passing. You mentioned that you did not see -- after you were stopped by two soldiers, and you passed and your brother and your neighbour (redacted) did not pass. Did you see them after that? Did you hear about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't hear or see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And your brother was a military man, and your neighbour (redacted), were they fighting with the BiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, no, they were not fighting. My brother was retired, and this neighbour of mine also worked in the same company where I worked, for the forestry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have just one question, Witness E. When Milisav Gavric gave into the hangar with General Mladic, was he wearing some kind of uniform? Gavric, was Gavric --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Gavric, I told you, he had a uniform, but I couldn't be more specific. It was blue or olive drab in colour. I couldn't tell you exactly. And Mladic, he was wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mladic was wearing civilian. And Gavric, you testified, I believe, was from around Srebrenica. He had worked in Srebrenica. That's how you knew him before; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew him. I told you that he was doing his internship in my company. And then after that, he went to school, and later on he joined the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know where Gavric is from. I don't know where he was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, do you remember how many times you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I believe I gave a statement on two occasions. This is my recollection of the things. Two times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember who you gave these statements to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, that, I don't remember. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, can you read and write?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I could write some Cyrillic script, but the thing is, I cannot see very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were giving your statements, do you remember whether you signed them or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I signed them or not. I couldn't tell you about that. I'm afraid I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember where exactly you gave those statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Once, I believe that I gave a statement in Zivinice, and the other one I think I gave it in Tuzla, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, as regards the statement that you gave in Tuzla, do you remember more or less the time when you gave that particular statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot remember the time. I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but perhaps you remember you were in Tuzla; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how long had you been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: You mean after I had arrived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that you had lived in Srebrenica, that you were there during the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So how did you reach Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what I would like to know is how much time had elapsed between your arrival in Tuzla and the time when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I forgot. I couldn't tell you that. I don't know how much time had elapsed between my arrival from Srebrenica and my giving that statement. I couldn't tell you that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness E, let me try to help you. Was it one day, one month, one year after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, more than a month. Perhaps a year since I arrived. But apart from that, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, Witness E. Were you alone or were you in the company of somebody when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I was alone. I remember that. I remember I was all by myself when I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the authorities, the body that took your statement, was it only one person there, or were there several individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There was one person who was there when they took my statement. I remember that. I was sitting at the table, and it stuck in my mind: there was one man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember where, in which building, in what kind of place did you make the statement in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know that. I couldn't tell you that. I don't remember. It's not in my mind anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness E. We have no further questions. Thank you very much for making this effort and giving your evidence here. Thank you. And we now wish you a happy, safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, perhaps it is time for a break, or shall we proceed, as we did before?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I take advantage, Mr. President, of a closed session, if it -- is it still closed, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the next witness, or if the Court wishes to have a break, we can do either, but I'd like to inform the Chamber of a misrepresentation that I made to the Chamber in respect of certain statements. And if I could go into closed session, I can inform the Chamber of some additional recent information that I got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon, you can speak openly, but I think we have to go into closed session. Are we? No. Excuse me. Let's organise things slightly differently. Let us first address things that we can address in open session and then go into closed session, in order not to have to go back and forward. So our next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our next witness is open; there are no protections requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, do you want to tender Exhibits 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know what the parties think, but exhibits should be tendered by deleting, by removing, the name of the witness, because the contents of the statement may be public, and the protection covers only the protection of the witness. So that these statements should be edited -- that is, the witness's name should be deleted -- and having done that, you may tender it under seal. What do you think, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Under seal for both exhibits is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't saying under seal; I was saying to tender them publicly, not under seal. But in order to protect the witness, we only need to strike out the name of the witness, which appears in the statement, who gave this statement. So the document will be accessible to the public, but the objective is to protect the witness and identity of the witness. So by producing this exhibit, one has to eliminate, to strike out the name, to redact the name, and the witness -- in this way, the document will not become damaging to the witness and then the document will become public. Do we understand that, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have not reviewed either of those statements, but oftentimes in the statement there is identifying information other than the name that needs to be redacted from the statement. He might state the name of his wife or the name of his children, or other information that can be equally harmful to a witness who has sought the protection of this Chamber. That's why my suggestion would be that the statement be placed under seal or, alternatively, we have an opportunity to review it, to redact, identifying information, and then it could be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Harmon. You will then read through the statement from the point of view of the witness's protection, and you will then tell us which are the parts which need to be redacted, and after that, the document will be tendered. That is the only concern of the Chamber, because our hearings are open, and that is a matter of principle. However, if we have a statement of a protected witness, if we protect the witness and make the document public, then we should do so. So, Mr. Harmon, you will read the statement and you will communicate it to the Defence, and the Chamber will then see that it is admitted with the redactions that you have made. Thank you very much. And now we shall move briefly into a closed session, because Mr. Harmon has a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are in open session so as to announce that the next witness will be giving his evidence in open session, and we shall now make a break. We do need a short rest, and Mr. Visnjic can read the statement so as to prepare for cross-examination. So a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness Vaasen. Could you please stand up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You are now going to read the solemn declaration, which the usher has already given to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. I think I should also hear the solemn declaration of our interpreter. Madam, could you please read out the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will do so faithfully, independently, impartially, and with full respect for the duty of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Witness Vaasen, the Tribunal is grateful for your appearance here. You are now going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Cayley, who is representing the Prosecution here. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. In order to clarify matters concerning the interpreter who is sitting to the right of Mr. Vaasen, Mr. Vaasen will testify in the English language. His English is excellent. He simply requires the presence of an interpreter in case there is anything at any point he doesn't understand in respect of questions that I put to him or questions, indeed, put by my learned friends, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your full name is David Vaasen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can spell that for the purposes of the transcript, that's V-a-a-s-e-n. Is that the correct spelling of your name?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are now 28 years of age?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are Dutch by nationality.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are presently a lance corporal in the Air Mobile Battalion of the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think your specialisation in the army is that you are a medical orderly. You're a medic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want you to cast your mind back to July of 1995, when I think you were then a private first class; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were also performing the duties of a medical orderly, a medic.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was with DutchBat III, based again in the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think at the time you were 23 years of age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Corporal Vaasen, at the beginning of July of 1995, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I was at an observation post called Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, next to you you'll see a large map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Usher, if that map could be brought in so the witness can more easily see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just point to the Judges your location at that time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I see. So that was your location in the beginning of July 1995. And if the record can show that the witness is pointing, or did point to Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E and is indicating Observation Post Mike, which is an orange circle marked "M" on the grey line which delineates the Srebrenica enclave. Thank you very much, Corporal Vaasen. You can take a seat. Can you tell the Judges what you recall of events at the beginning of July whilst you were located at Observation Post Mike?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the last couple of days were very intense. We had some mortar fire near our observation post. The first couple of days were one, maybe two single shells, and they put it up more and more every day. So we had to stay in the bunker for almost three days, and after that, we were called by the Serbs to come out and to leave our observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They shouted at us and used also a lot of things to make themselves clear that we had to move away from our observation post because they were going to bomb it with mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've just said in your evidence that "we had some mortar fire near our observation post." Who, to your knowledge, fired those mortars at Observation Post Mike?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: That was the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've just stated that the Serbs asked you to withdraw because they threatened you with more mortar fire. What did your unit that was based at OP Mike do after those threats were made?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: First, our group commander took the radio and gave all the messages through to the base and Potocari, and then they told us later to withdraw ourselves to about 100 metres nearby the village Jaglici, and to stay up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate on Prosecution Exhibit 1E the village, if it's marked on that map, to which you withdrew?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Jaglici [Indicates], here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the camera could zoom in, because I can't see through the lectern there. Thank you. Let the record show that the witness is indicating on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E to the village called Jaglici.
