utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could take a seat again, Corporal Vaasen. Could you tell the Judges what happened when you got to Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: When we arrived at Jaglici, we were stopped by the Muslim army. They were under Captain Enwer, and they forced us to stay there, even with violence if necessary, and we were going to go back to our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did they want you to stay in Jaglici? Why did, as you term it, the Muslim army want you to stay in Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, because we were the UN army there, and also for their protection, and also to use our equipment, if it's necessary, against the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "an army," when you first got to Jaglici, how many Muslim soldiers did you see with Captain Enwer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, he was a local officer, he was the local commander there, and there were also Muslim soldiers of -- I can't recall now but from the 82nd Muslim Brigade -- that's how they called themselves -- and there were approximately about 30, 40 Muslim soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your recollection, do you recall how they were armed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, not so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're a professional soldier. We are not. If you could explain to the Judges what you mean by "not so good"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, some of them had guns, pistols, and they didn't have enough ammunition to fight for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these Muslim soldiers essentially wished you to remain in Jaglici. How long did you remain in Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: For three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At the end of three days, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Sorry. It was so that we tried to go away there. Our group commander, he was speaking to Captain Enwer, the local commander, and he made an arrangement that we could go back to our base in Potocari but we had to take women, children, and older people with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that you had to take -- that Captain Enwer asked you to take women, children, and older people with you. Where were these women, children, and older people from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were, first of all, from Jaglici and also from other houses near Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So at the end of this three-day period, you make your way back to Potocari. Can you tell the Judges about that journey back to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, when we started to drive back to our base, we had people behind our APC, armoured personnel carrier, also on our armoured personnel carrier, and the crowd went larger and larger by the second because there also came Muslim people from out of the mountains, and they joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you, from your recollection, tell the Judges what state those people were in?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were in very bad shape. They didn't have any water, no food, hardly any clothes. They were terrified, you could see it, and it was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, as you approached the cemetery on the route that you took back, can you tell the Judges what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I saw Muslim soldiers. It was like they were coming together there, and it was a huge crowd, and they were also armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall how many Muslim soldiers you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: A couple of hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you stand up again? I'm sorry to keep asking you to sit down and stand up, but, unfortunately, this courtroom is not well designed for using large exhibits. Could you indicate to the Judges the route that you took from Jaglici to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, again, if the camera could zoom in so that I could actually see what the witness is pointing at.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]. This is where we started, and we were driving down from the hills, towards Potocari. And here is the cemetery [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So am I correct in saying that you drove the length of that road that is marked on the exhibit between, I think, Susnjari, Jaglici, and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate once more the location of the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Right here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you keep the marker there?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show the witness is indicating the route that he took from Jaglici to Potocari, being the road marked inside the Srebrenica enclave from Jaglici, through Susnjari, to Potocari, and the cemetery being an approximate location just above the "J" in Susnjari on the road between Susnjari and Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you can take a seat again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, sorry to interrupt you. So that we have everything clear, did they stop on the left or on the right side of the road? This might assist us in finding the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, whether the cemetery that you saw, and bearing in mind the direction that you were going in -- you were actually moving from Susnjari to Potocari -- whether it was on the left-hand side of the road or the right-hand side of the road?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It was on the left hand from the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Do you recall what time of the day that you were making this journey?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, it was already later that day, because it got a little bit darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges what happened when you reached Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: When we reached Potocari, our commanding officer in Potocari told us to stay right near Potocari, and we couldn't -- first of all, we couldn't go back to the base because the refugees who were coming from Srebrenica had first to go to Potocari and they wanted to organise that thing first before we went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that your commanding officer told you to stay right near Potocari. Can you remember approximately what distance you stopped from the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: From the UN compound, it's about one -- one and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that it was on the road between Susnjari and Potocari that you stopped 100 metres short of the intersection, so that you don't have to get up again?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened when you stopped at that location?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: When we stopped at that location, we had to wait there, and after a couple of minutes, we took heavy fire from the left of us, and it was total chaos. They were shooting at us. They were shooting at the Muslim people who were behind us and also in front of us. The crowd started to run, to shout, and we also tried to help the people, and we also had to leave the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what was your job in the APC at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I was the shooter from the .50-calibre Browning, gun-crew member.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My learned friend has just pointed out perhaps something that I've confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're saying that you were one and a half kilometres from the UN compound. If you could stand up -- and we're going to have to use the map because I think it's probably easier -- and if you could show the Judges where you were located.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the camera could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were about one and a half kilometres from the UN base at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E, on the road between Susnjari to the UN base, just to the left of the purple triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, how far was that location from the intersection with the Potocari road?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: About 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You can take a seat now. Now, you said that you essentially were on the gun crew for the .50-calibre Browning, and at that point in time, you were actually taking direct fire. Do you know who you were taking direct fire from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: From the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think your rules of engagement allowed you to return fire when directly engaged. Did you return fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you not return fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because I also had Muslim people on the APC, and if I fired that weapon, it would harm them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you describe a chaotic occurrence where the Muslims that were in and around the APC panicked. How many people were around you at that point? How many refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: A couple of hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see where they ran to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They went towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you then continued along that road, and you then ran into another APC from the UN. Can you tell the Judges what happened when you ran into that other APC?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: When we arrived at the intersection, there was from the Bravo Company an APC who stopped us and gave us the direction and also the order to leave the Muslim people at the factory, and we had to go back to the base and take the injured people with us, the injured Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So where did you leave the Muslim refugees who were not injured? Can you remember the location in and around Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Near the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/9, please. If that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. What is the Bravo Company he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: The Bravo Company was the other company that was stationed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's a military division?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is it a military division?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No. It's a company; it's no division. It's also from the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify matters, Corporal Vaasen, how many companies were there that operated on the company from DutchBat III?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: We had Bravo Company stationed in Srebrenica, and we were stationed, the Potocari Company, in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But I'm right in saying that platoons from those two companies were located in all of the various observation posts and, indeed, in Potocari itself and in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Charlie Company, was it responsible for a geographical sector of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which sector was it responsible for?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It was a northerly direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Bravo Company was responsible for which section?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: South.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, is that reasonably clear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: For the moment, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Corporal Vaasen -- Mr. Usher, if you could move it, because I think he's going to have difficulty reaching across. Could you please point on that exhibit to the location of the bus station?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]. This whole building, and also here, where the buses are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could leave the pointer in the middle of the bus complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, for the purposes of the record, the witness is pointing to Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/9 and indicating to the large building in the background, a large grey building which dominates the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Now, after you had left the refugees at the bus station and taken the wounded into the compound, as you said, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: First of all, we had to drive our APC into the fabric, and -- factory, I'm sorry, into the factory, and we also helped the medics up there to load off those Muslim people off our vehicle, and we also had to return to our commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you'd done all of that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I took a meal and I went to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to "the factory," you're referring to the DutchBat UN compound?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move to the next day, which I believe was the 12th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened on that day, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. I got up very early in the morning, and they needed some soldiers to go to check out how the situation was outside. There already were UN soldiers outside. So we went on patrol with the commanding officer -- I don't know his name anymore -- and we left the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you left the base, can you describe the scene that you saw to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, it was terrible, because people were crying and -- I'm sorry. They were -- they didn't have any water, no food. They were grabbing at us to help them, and we stayed at the -- first of all, at the first factory. We also went inside there to check it --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, Witness. Do you recall approximately how many people you could see all around you as you walked out of the compound?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: A couple of thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what the temperature was at that time of day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, it was very -- it was already getting hotter by the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you walked out of the camp and that you went to the first factory. Do you recall the name of that factory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: We called it the Blue/White Factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/19.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the Blue Factory on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point to the Blue Factory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/19 and indicating to a factory building in the right background of the photograph that is, in fact, blue in colour and has a structure, a small structure, built on the roof of it. There's a small square structure, a rectangular structure, on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate where the UN compound is located?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. Up here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness is pointing to the building in the left background of Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/19.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Could you tell the Judges what you saw and sensed as you went into that building?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: When we went inside, we saw also Muslim refugees, and on the look on their face, they were very terrified. Most of them were also crying. And the feeling that you get, it's -- it was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what else you saw in that building on the morning of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: There were also Muslim people who had hanged themselves because they were -- yeah, by my feeling, terrified that something was going on. And the Muslim refugees who were also there didn't look at them, didn't do anything. It looked like they were in a state of shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were some Muslim people who had hanged themselves, and I know these memories are difficult for you, but can you describe to the Judges exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They used everything to hang themselves. It was not a rope. Some of them took some clothes or something else; I cannot recall. By the look of it, it was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you saw these bodies hanging there, what did you and your fellow soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: We took them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what did you do with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: We took them outside the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these individuals who had hanged themselves, do you remember their sex, whether they were male or female, how old they were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Most of them were male.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know how many bodies you cut down that morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you say most of them were male. Were they both men?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Approximately what age?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, they looked older than they were, but my feeling was that they were about 30, 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the refugees in the rest of the building, you said they looked as if they were in a state of shock. How were they composed? Were they men, women, and children, or were there more of one particular group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, there were more women and children than men up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were the ages of the children that you saw in the Blue Factory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, it was from a baby, so from zero to 16, 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these bodies were just hanging there in front of these children and these women?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to me anything else that was significant that you sensed in that building when you walked in?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- you could smell that they had urinated there; also they had defecated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you said that they had urinated in the building.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what else did you say they had done in the building? I didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They defecated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you'd moved around the Blue Factory, do you recall where you went next?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. Our commanding officer told us to mix up our group. We each went in a different kind of direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I went to the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, indeed, is the bus station that you indicated earlier on the photograph that I showed to you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you find at the bus station?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: More Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was their state?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were all in the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "the same state," do you mean the same as the people in the Blue Factory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you'd been to the bus compound, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, we went more towards our own UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you are medically trained.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're a medical orderly. How did you feel when you looked around at all of these people?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, I could tell that they were in bad shape, really bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you do anything for them, as a medic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, not directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because we didn't have enough equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you returned to the compound, do you recall what your next orders required you to do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, I had to stay outside by my -- yeah, we called it the beginning of where the refugees were standing, or lying or sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall where you stayed outside? Do you recall where you were located?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was in front of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think at some stage you were instructed by your unit to form a human chain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what time this human chain was formed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Let me see, it was about 2.00, 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you give the approximate location?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're indicating on the road that runs north to south on this photograph, are you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the human chain was -- now, this is the first human chain, is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it's approximately between the location marked "The Zinc Factory" and the "Faros Building" about halfway in between, and that's on Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2. Can you explain to the Judges what exactly that human chain was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: That human chain was with UN soldiers, we had to stay there because the Serb army was coming into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you formed a line across the road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. You can take your hand away from that photograph now. How many soldiers were there on the first barricade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: About 40 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In what position was your weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I had to hold it on my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you have to put your weapon on your back?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Our orders were not to be aggressive to the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were placed in this position because the Serb army was coming to the enclave. How long after you formed this human chain did the Serb army come to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Right directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall where they came from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They came from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sir, if you could indicate on the photograph again the direction from which they came, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's this road [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating from the bottom, the southern point of the photograph, along the road that runs down the middle towards Potocari, so upwards from the bottom of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the soldiers that you saw, these soldiers that arrived from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were heavily armed. They had many weapons with them. They had, we call it, RPGs, that's an anti-tank weapon. They had AK-47s with them. They had sidearms with them, machine-guns. There was also a Russian-type tank coming also.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you described how they were armed. Can you describe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: The first group that entered were dressed in black.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's stay with that first group that were dressed in black. Can you tell the Judges what you know about that group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, when we saw them, and they were standing right in front of us, you could see that they were from the Arkan Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that they were from Arkan's Tigers. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because before we went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had training to remember the Serb soldiers, how they are dressed, and the Muslim soldiers, and by that way, we knew that they were Arkan's Tigers, and one of them also told us that they were Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did one of them tell you that he was from the Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Also to me and friends of mine, colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any significant badge or insignia that indicated the unit?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. They had also a badge with a tiger on it, and the regular Serb badge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you actually directly speak to any of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, yes. Some of them speak English, some of them speak German, and I also speak a little bit of German, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is the first group that you saw. What other groups did you see coming from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Also regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say "regular soldiers," can you describe the uniforms that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how were they armed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were also real good armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any other units that came from Bratunac that you could identify?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say the Drina Wolves. How do you know that they were the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because when they were right in front of us, they had a badge with a wolf on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this badge, Corporal Vaasen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what is this badge?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It's the badge from the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, within the Drina Wolves unit, do you recall how many soldiers you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, about 50, 60 the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How well armed were the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Very good, heavily armed, just like the Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say that there were essentially three units that arrived at this time: the Arkan Tigers, the Drina Wolves, and regular VRS soldiers.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did they all appear to be working together, coming up towards the human barricade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, no, no. They all had their own commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when they arrived at the barrier, how did the refugees react to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were very scared because they were aware of the Arkan Tigers and the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after these two special units and these regular soldiers arrived at your barricade, do you recall what happened next?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were some Drina Wolves, they were going to some houses on the left of me and started to plunder those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges, when you say they started to plunder those houses, what exactly you saw taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, the first couple of houses where they went in, they came out with not really useful things, telephones, typewriters, coffee machines. They took everything. And after a couple of houses, they also went inside another house, and they -- you could hear a scream, you heard a burst from an AK-47. After that, they also came out with stuff from inside, so also another telephone, VCR player, and thrown a grenade inside. We called it a phosphor grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you could hear a scream and you heard a burst from an AK-47. At the time, what did you think was taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: That they were killing those people inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, as far as you know, were there members of the Bosnian army based in and around those houses near Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there members of the Muslim army in those houses --

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, no, not from the Muslim army, just refugees, people who stayed there and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So as far as you know, the Muslims in those houses were refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that you saw them throw a phosphor grenade, and I think by this you mean a phosphorus grenade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when that phosphorus grenade was thrown into the house, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you saw this taking place, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: We approached those Serb soldiers and tried to stop them. They laughed at us, and even one of them told us to stand down, not to interfere with what they were doing, that it's no problem to kill one or two people more, and they were pointing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, how many times did you see this taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: A couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "a couple," you can be more specific, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/19, and if the photograph could actually be moved up. Further, actually. We don't need to have the factories actually particularly in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a photograph that I've previously shown you. Can you explain to the Judges whether you recognise this photograph in connection with the incidents that you've just described to them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. Where those houses are up here [indicates], they started first to walk up here [indicates]. They took this house, that house, and started here to throw hand grenades inside [indicates], to shoot people, and they walked on, so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you could just indicate again, first of all, where the soldiers walked from when they --

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So I'm correct in saying they left the main road just by the Blue Factory, and the red building, the red house without a roof to the right of the photograph, and they walked up the path, and then they cleared a number of these houses that you're indicating to in the foreground, a number of these civilian houses which are quite clearly shown on the exhibit in the foreground. How many times did you see this activity take place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, with the hand grenades was three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the shooting and hearing the screaming? How many times did you hear and see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: One time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Now, when you saw this taking place, how did you feel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I felt very sick in my stomach. It's not a normal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you'd already been warned, you've explained to the Judges, by one of these Serb soldiers not to get involved. So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I went back to the human barricade and told the commander officer what's going on up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: He said, "Okay. You had better not do anything," because at the moment when I saw that, I was very angry. First of all, I was wanting to grab my weapon and shoot them, but I couldn't do that because you also have think about the other Muslim people that were there then and also about your colleagues. There are several things that you have to think about. And in the state of those Serb soldiers, I don't think that they could think very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why do you think they could not think very clearly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because from the moment they went inside, you could smell alcohol. They were using drugs. So they were under the influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say that they were using drugs, how could you tell?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because I smelled it and I saw it a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What could you see?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were sniffing white powder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're a medic. Do you have any idea what drugs that they were using?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Cocaine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you returned, you said, to the human barricade. What did you see when you got back to the barricade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, when I was there, later on there were some cars approaching to the UN compound and the barricade, and a couple of soldiers came out and also General Mladic with some bodyguards, and other high-rank soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time this was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It was already later that day. It was about 3.00, 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say you saw General Mladic and some other high-ranking soldiers. What did General Mladic do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: First of all, he approached the Muslim refugees, and there was also a camera crew with him, and they started to throw candy into the Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just stop there, and we'll play a section of video which I think will probably help you refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 3. It's a thirty-second video clip. If the video could be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can stop at that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Corporal Vaasen, do you recall that scene?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that the soldiers were throwing candy to the children.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, indeed, as this shows, all of this was being filmed. Can you explain to the Judges what happened immediately after this took place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they were filming everything that General Mladic was telling something to the people, and the people in front of them were a little bit, yeah, how do you call it, scared. And he tried to shake hands with the people, and then the cameraman switched off the camera. And what then happened was terrible because he took the candy back, kicked the people, even hit those children up front.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say "he took the candy back." Who took the candy back from the children?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, they took them back, those soldiers who were in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these soldiers, these were members of the Bosnian Serb army that were around General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recall anything else that you saw at that time, immediately after the camera switched off?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, you saw that those faces were really terrified, of those Muslim people, and directly he gave orders to a man who was right in front -- on the right of him, and that person went away. He let those other officers from the Serb soldiers come to him, he talked to them, and those Serb officers went back to their own unit, and they started to reorganise things. They were starting to stand left and right of the road --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Corporal Vaasen, if I can just interrupt you here. You said that -- in response to my question, "Directly he gave orders to a man who was right in front." Who gave orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic, let's focus on him for a moment. Whilst all this is going on, the candy is being taken back from the children, people were being kicked, what was General Mladic doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: He was standing there and he looked very superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he see what his soldiers were doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he say or do anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the man to whom he gave orders, did you know his name, the man to whom Mladic gave orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, but I can recall his face. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President. Ah, it's a good time to take a break, Mr. President, I think you're indicating to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. We shall take a 15-minute break, so as not to have too long a period of work at a stretch. Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you. If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/13 and 28/13.1, please, which is the compilation of photographs of various individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these are photographs which I've previously shown to you. If you could identify the individuals on this photograph, this is 28/13, you can go ahead and identify the individuals on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: This man [indicates] is General Mladic, and this is the other person I had seen with General Mladic, near those Muslim refugees. This is the same person who got orders from Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show on Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/13 that the individual on the left of the photograph, the witness is identifying as General Mladic, and the individual on the right-hand photograph as the other person who the witness saw with General Mladic near to the Muslim refugees and who received orders from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely sure, Corporal Vaasen, this is the individual that you were speaking of before the break who received orders from Mladic immediately after the incident with the women and the children, and the candy, the throwing of the candy.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, once these orders were given to the individual that you recognised, can you explain to the Court what happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb soldiers were reorganising, and they were going to stand to the left and right of the road. After that, I saw the man who took the orders from Mladic grab a small radio, talk into the radio, and after a couple of minutes, trucks and buses came into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, while these Serb soldiers were reorganising, how were the refugees reacting at this point?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were really scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other VRS soldiers at that time who you hadn't seen previously?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. The first vehicle that approached the refugees was full of Serb soldiers with German Shepherds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say "German Shepherds," you don't mean shepherds of German origin, you mean the breed of dog that is a German Shepherd.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did these soldiers with these dogs do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, each soldier had his own dog, and they also took a side, the left side or the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when the refugees were in and around these soldiers with the dogs, did you see anything taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. They started to put the Muslim people inside those trucks and inside those buses and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: And they also -- separation took place at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say that separation took place, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I mean men from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when these men were separated, where did you see them being taken?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: There was a building, we called it the White House, and they were taken to that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did the refugees react when they were separated, when families were separated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It was total chaos. People tried to run away, push each other away, and whenever that happened, they started to fire in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say "they started to fire in the air," who started to fire in the air?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Some Muslim soldiers who were in front of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that Muslim soldiers started to fire who were in front of the --

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm sorry. Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So Serb soldiers started to fire in the air above the refugees.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: With what weapon did they fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: With their AK-47s, all kinds of weapons, and they even had a machine-gun placed on some kind of balcony, in a house, and they shot over their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to give the Judges an approximate location of where all of this was taking place, do you recall where this was taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was still near the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on that road --

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: On that road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- near to the bus station. Now, how did the crowd react when the Serb soldiers started firing over the heads of the crowd?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They started to scream, to shout. Some of them who didn't listen got even directly fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say, "Some of them who didn't listen even got directly fire." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were shooting at the person directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So VRS soldiers were shooting directly at individuals in the crowd.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was anybody injured as a result of this shooting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. I even helped two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you are a medic, you were a medic. Do you recall the injuries of those people?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One was shot in the leg and the other one was also shot in the leg and in the stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the sex of those who were injured?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Female.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were both of them females?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you describe to the Judges, you started to explain the process of separation and moving the refugees onto the buses, can you describe how that process took place and what you saw happening, what you saw the VRS soldiers doing around these refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, when they started to move those refugees to the buses and the trucks, they were -- well, it was very, very hard. Some of them were even kicked, beaten. They used their weapons, the back of the weapon, to hit them everywhere. And even by the separation of the men, that was even harder because children tried to grab their fathers, even their brothers, and they used even force up there to separate those men, and they pushed the women and the children towards the bus and the men towards the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the human barricade, you stated, was next to the bus station. Did it remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges where the human barricade moved to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 5/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall at approximately what time the barricade moved?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I don't. I don't recall that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did the barricade move?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because we were totally outnumbered up there, and there were so many refugees that we couldn't have held them in one place, and that's why they pushed us towards the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've given the wrong number. Can the witness be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what you're saying is, in essence, you were actually physically pushed back down the road.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate as best you can remember, and I know it's a long time ago now, but approximately to where the barricade moved on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So this is the second location of the barricade, the first being opposite the bus compound.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: The first one was here [indicates], and then it moved 300 metres down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating on Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2, to the right of the wording "Faros Building," on the road that runs north/south, like a ribbon, down the centre of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Corporal Vaasen, the barricade was still actually on the road.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you describe, when you looked into these buses that were around, can you describe to the Judges the condition of the refugees in those buses?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, the refugees were in totally bad shape. It was even very hot that day, about 38 degrees. The people who went inside those buses and trucks were pushed inside, and even you could see that they were putting too many people -- too many people in one vehicle because you saw even those children, their heads against the window, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you saw this, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. I walked back, because I walked several times with some of those Muslims, I walked back to that man who earlier was given those orders from Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's the man that you recognised in the photograph with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you walked back to that man, and did you find him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, yes, yes. He was standing all the time at the same place, and I told him that there were too many people in one bus or in a truck, and he told me that it was not his concern and we had to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when he said that you had to deal with it, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I went back to the commander officer, who was standing right in front of the human chains, and I told him what was going on at the buses. So we started to reorganise the human chain, and they let, every time, groups of ten people go out of crowd towards those buses. Some of the soldiers who were UN soldiers even got orders from that person to walk with them, and if you see that there were enough people in the bus, stop it and then go directly to the other bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you're referring to the commanding officer, are you referring to the Dutch commanding officer or a Bosnian Serb officer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, it was our commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The Dutch commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in essence, you're saying that by reorganising the human chain, you regulated the flow of refugees, you controlled the flow. You took less people who were coming through the barricade to get on the buses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you yourself actually escort any of these groups to buses?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did conditions get better when you put this plan into effect --

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- for the refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did it get better?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because those buses were not so full that they were -- that they had also their faces against the windows, and they even could sit normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's just talk again at this point about the Bosnian Serb army that was in and around this operation that was taking place. Can you describe the uniforms of the Bosnian Serb soldiers at this point in time, who were in and around the refugees and the buses?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They wore all camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Green camouflage or blue camouflage?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Green.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier special units and regular Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At this point in time, these large groups of VRS soldiers, were they regulars or special units?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: No, they were regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's talk about the White House, which you mentioned earlier. You said that you saw men being separated and taken to the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness can be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again, this is a photograph that I've shown you earlier. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what that photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: It shows the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is the White House to which you were referring where men were taken off to the separation from their families?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges what you saw taking place at the White House from your vantage point at the human barricade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: The men who were separated from their families had to go through the gate. Right in front of it you have a gate here [indicates]. They had to sit right in front of it, beside this house [indicates], and they had to leave all their luggage also here on the grass. Some of them were also taken inside to the house, and later on they came out and they were -- you could see that there was something going on, because they had scars, bruises, everything, and they got separated from the rest of the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Approximately how far away from the White House were you when you were observing the events taking place there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a little bit of the main road [indicates], and I was standing here [indicates] and later here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating to the left of the foreground to the main road that you can see. The main road leads into the side road into the White House. He was standing at the entrance to the side road, observing what was taking place at the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit more about the men that you saw. Do you recall anything else of the men that you saw outside the White House?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. The men were very scared. Some of them were in some kind of shock. They were staring only right in front of them. Some of them even cried. It was real bad, their look was real bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the evacuation that day, on the 12th, for how long did it continue?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Until it got dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when it got dark and the evacuation stopped, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "there," where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: I stayed near the human barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you stay at the human barricade all night, or did you go around the area? Did you look into any of the other buildings around that area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: We also got orders to check the buildings, and the refugees, what kind of state they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you go that night? Can you tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes. We also went -- excuse me. We also went, first of all, to the Blue Factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that the Blue Factory that you previously identified in a photograph that I showed to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, from your memory, exactly what you saw that night in the Blue Factory, what you heard, what you smelt?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, it was the same smell as the whole day -- as earlier that day, when I went inside, and people were scared. Some of them were starving from hunger, and they didn't have any water. Even we couldn't help them. It was very dark inside. And behind the factory, we heard some crazy noises, so we checked it out. We were with three members, three UN soldiers, and we went to the back of the factory, and when we were at that area, we heard the sound of a female. And we switched our flashlights on, and we saw two Serb soldiers, one of them was standing guard and the other one was lying on the girl, with his pants off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you got there and switched the flashlight on, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, they were -- first of all, they didn't know who we were, and they started to run away. And it was so quickly that, even for us, it was a surprise because we didn't know what we were getting into. And we saw a girl lying on the ground, on some kind of mattress. There was blood on the mattress, even she was covered with blood. She had bruises on her legs. There was even blood coming down her legs. She was in total shock. She went totally crazy. We even tried, in her language, to calm her down, but she didn't listen. Well, we had to take her outside, and outside the building we were helped by female Muslim refugees who told us to keep the woman with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were a medic. Did you offer medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, I tried, but they refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did they refuse?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Because she was totally in shock. She was also kicking towards us and waving with her hands. And she didn't want help from us because she was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, at the time, and I'm going to ask you a question that seems fairly obvious, but it's for the purposes of the record, did you conclude what you had seen taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, a raping.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there other refugees in and around this rape while it was taking place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: They were sitting on the ground. They couldn't do anything because the Serb soldiers were covering them with weapons. And after those scenes, what we had seen that day, I thought myself that they would use it against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How old was the girl? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID VAASEN
utterances.text: Well, she was very young, about 19, 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you wish to end at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much longer do you think your examination-in-chief will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Another 15 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then perhaps it is better to adjourn now. Very well. We shall adjourn and resume tomorrow with your testimony, Mr. Vaasen. We shall be resuming tomorrow at half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of March, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 25
